title: Cempaka Seri: rethinking the townhouse.
videoTitle: PROPERTY REVIEW #150 | CEMPAKA SERI, KOTA SERIEMAS
excerpt: A townhouse that answers the three complaints the format usually attracts — narrow entry, tangled structure and dark corners — inside a township that spent its land on infrastructure.
takeaways: A four-foot staircase sounds like a small decision, but it removes the objection most buyers have to townhouses: getting furniture upstairs.
The double-height living space lights the unit without artificial light, and a slit window carries that daylight into the bedrooms above.
The township spent twenty years building lakes, cycle paths and mature tree cover on land it could have sold instead.

sections.heading: A township that started in 2000
paragraphs: Sean sets the coordinates first. Kota Seriemas sits beside Nilai, within reach of Seremban and close to the airport, connected between the expressway network and the North–South Highway. It is a master plan of more than 2,400 acres that began in the year 2000 and, at the time of filming, was still going strong two decades on.

The buyer profile follows the geography. Aviation workers based at the airport have long been the core market, with a second group commuting to the administrative capital as an alternative to living there.

He notes the two approaches carefully, because they leave opposite impressions. Arrive by the highway and you meet an entrance statement and well-built infrastructure. Arrive through the older village roads and the impression is very different — one of his later concerns.

sections.heading: Land that was not sold
paragraphs: Before the product, Sean tours the amenities, and this is where his admiration sits. The township carries a golf and country club, a university college hosting around two thousand students, and a quarters area with grocers, laundries, workshops and gyms — several thousand homes' worth of supporting population for the commercial strip.

The infrastructure is the argument. Roads run three lanes wide under mature tree cover, with dedicated bicycle and jogging paths, bicycle parking, hedged bus stops for safety and a recreational lake with lotus planting and an elevated play structure. His episode notes add that the township has been recognised with landscape and build-quality awards.

His point is blunt: all of that land could have been converted into sellable plots, and he is glad it was not. When you buy a location, he argues, you are not only buying a plot — you are buying the amenities and infrastructure around it, because that is what forms your lifestyle. The contrast with what sits immediately outside the perimeter is what makes it visible.

sections.heading: How the townhouses are arranged
paragraphs: Cempaka Seri is a townhouse on a 24 by 70 ft lot, which means each unit gets a single car opening at the front. What makes the scheme unusual is that the architects worked with the existing topography rather than flattening it, so the blocks step with the land.

A landscaped drainage corridor cuts through the development, splitting it in two and giving genuine breathing space between the buildings. Units are grouped in fours with planting between the rows, and there is usable space behind each house.

The practical details are handled: drainage is concealed, which he notes is safer with children around, and car parks are covered with canopies alongside the feeder pillars, street lighting and planting. Because this is a strata development, community living remains part of the design — neighbours can greet each other across the arrangement, and it ventilates across.

sections.heading: The staircase that solves the format
paragraphs: The unit filmed is the upper-floor type. Entry gathers the utility meters and refuse compartment to one side, with room to park two cars along the length, and opens onto a store room at the front — placed there, Sean notes, precisely because heavy things belong at ground level: golf clubs, bicycles, anything you would rather not carry up.

Then comes the detail he rates most highly. The staircase is four feet wide, with timber treads and steel handrails. That width is a direct answer to the single biggest objection people raise about townhouses — moving furniture upstairs. At four feet, it stops being a problem.

Upstairs the plan opens into the kitchen and dry yard, then the dining and living areas with a balcony facing the park; a further flight leads to three bedrooms. The courtyard carries the washing machine position with water inlet and floor trap already set, tiled with matching skirting, beside the air-conditioner ledge.

sections.heading: Six metres of daylight
paragraphs: The living space is the reason the unit works. It runs about 3.5 m wide and rises roughly 6 m as a double-height volume, and Sean points out that with no artificial lighting switched on the room is fully lit. In a corner unit, a side window adds even more.

That volume solves the townhouse's usual complaint of dark interiors, and it does so without complicating the structure — he calls the structural arrangement tidy and the column thickness pleasant, which for this format is not a given.

Pricing discussed in the episode put this unit around RM380,000 for roughly 1,800 sq ft, with lower units renting near RM1,500 a month. Those figures reflect the recording date in early 2021 and one specific type.

sections.heading: Bedrooms lit from the void
paragraphs: Two of the three bedrooms share a bathroom finished with full-height tiling and, in a pattern Sean keeps noticing, not one but two windows for ventilation, with obscured glazing preserving privacy.

The first bedroom carries timber flooring under a three-metre ceiling with its own balcony that opens on both sides, encouraging air to move right through the space. He also notes the window treatment differs deliberately between panels.

The principal bedroom measures about 3.5 by 4 m, and its best feature is an opening onto the double-height void — borrowing both the light and the park view from a different level. A slit window adds more brightness still, and Sean names it his single favourite detail in the house.

pros: The spatial arrangement and build quality answer every standard townhouse complaint: no narrow pinched entrance, no tangled structural arrangement, no dark corners, with the store room sensibly placed downstairs for heavy loads.
The balance between built-up and open space is unusually good, with organic block arrangement responding to the natural level changes rather than flattening them.

The pricing makes sense for the space and the position — roughly RM380,000 for about 1,800 sq ft near Nilai and the airport, with tertiary education on the doorstep and workable rental for the lower units.
cons: The pandemic had badly affected the aviation industry, which supplies the core group of buyers for this location.
The approach matters: arriving by highway you never notice, but the route through the older village roads leaves the impression of undeveloped land.
This is firmly an own-stay product. It lacks the commercial activity and bustle of the city — quiet enough, he notes, that the neighbour's television is audible.

closing: Cempaka Seri is the rare townhouse that reads as a considered house rather than a compromise, and the township around it has spent twenty years earning that setting. Whether it suits you comes down to one question Sean asks himself out loud: it makes complete sense if you work at the airport, and very little if you would be driving to the city every morning.
sourceNote: Based on Sean's full public English captions and his published YouTube episode notes. Measurements, unit size, price and rental figures are as discussed in the video and reflect the recording date in March 2021. The 3 on 3 section paraphrases the three things Sean says he likes and the three he has concerns about, presented near the end of the episode.
